validator: Draft 1 passes tools/eval/validate.mjs with no problems, soft points or warnings, so every fault below is the critic's, not the validator's.
keep: The idea named in one line up front: split a year's growth into more and more parts and the total settles on a fixed number, e.

The brief's picture, Split the year, with one named control stepping through 1, 2, 4, 12, 365 parts, and the table computed from (1 + 1/n)ⁿ rather than quoted (the brief notes the limit came back garbled in the research).
Toronto [1] on 'multiplied by e' and Mathwords [2] on e as a fixed constant like π, each on words its quote supports.
The worked example (£2,000 at 4% for 5 years, e^0.2) computed from the rule.
fix: Causal step skipped: why splitting helps at all. Two halves give £225, not £200, because the second half's 50% is taken of £150, not £100. Say it, then build (1 + 1/n)ⁿ from it: each part multiplies by 1 + 1/n and there are n of them, the A × bˣ of the last lesson.

Causal step skipped: why the total settles rather than running away. Show more parts helping less and less (365 to 8,760 parts adds only 36p) and give the reason, each extra split adding interest on ever smaller slices of interest, without the word 'never' (the brief: the table settles, with no 'never').

Causal step skipped, and the lesson's main claim taught as a bare statement: 'At rate k, growth that never pauses gives eᵏᵗ' has no why. Build it: 5% split into 100 parts gives each part 0.05%, the same as 100% split into 2,000 parts, and 100 of 2,000 is a twentieth of that year, so a year at 5% is e^(1/20) = e^0.05 ≈ 1.0513. Then eᵗ for 100% comes first, worked on the eˣ key (e² ≈ 7.389).

Misconception from the brief not caught: rate against factor (Mathwords, notes 6.3). The lesson must say k is not the growth factor (the factor per unit of time is eᵏ, 1.0513 for 5%, a little more than 1.05 paid once) and a DO screen must ask for the factor per year of e^(0.05t), with 0.05 and 1.05 as slips with their own hints.
False absolute risk: the takeaway's footnote [1] is put on the eᵏᵗ half, which Toronto's quote does not say. Keep [1] on 'multiplied by e' only.

Decay with a minus in the power is one line with no numbers. Show e^(−t) leaving 0.368, 0.135 and 0.050 after 1, 2 and 3 units, the same factor each equal step as in the last lesson, and point to the next lesson's capacitor without teaching RC.

The brief's last screen, the slope tracker preview, is missing. Add it as a look ahead: slope equals height on eˣ (textbooks add, unfootnoted, since notes 4.13 is not in this lesson's research), tied to OpenStax [3], the rate of growth proportional to the current value, and say nothing later depends on it.

Interactive brief and whatAmILookingAt name no screens, so the builder must guess them. List all thirteen: SHOW 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 13; DO 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; mixed 11 and 12, each wrong option with the slip that makes it, and the rate slider screen 7 needs. The numbers list lacks every slip value, the 5% table, e^0.5, e², e^(−1), e^(−2), e^(−3) and the tracker's readings.

ignores is thin: it should say what the staircase wrongly suggests (the flat treads are the time between payments, the smooth curve is the rule, not a balance) and that things made of whole pieces fit a smooth eᵏᵗ well only when there are many pieces.
Practice lacks a rule of thumb, a check against paying once, and the mistakes' numbers (e^20 for typing the rate as 4, 2,000 × e × 0.2 ≈ £1,087.31 for multiplying instead of raising).

No analogy. One from Dan's work reproduces the main result: straight lengths of trunking round a curved wall, more and shorter lengths hugging the curve, the total length settling. Its break: the extra length comes from geometry, not from interest earning interest.

round2.fixed: All eleven points above are fixed in draft 2.
checked: No false absolutes: the total 'settles on' e and 'more parts help less and less'; 'for ever without repeating' is said of e's decimals as a textbook fact; 'the same factor on every equal step' holds for e^(−t) at every setting.
Every number is a control, an assumed example worded 'say', computed from (1 + 1/n)ⁿ, eᵏᵗ or e^(−kt) on screen, or e itself, cited to Mathwords [2].

Misconceptions caught on DO screens with their own hints: adding the split parts (2), growth running away with more parts (4), multiplying by the time instead of raising (6), rate taken as the factor and paid-once factor (8), the minus dropped and decay taken as a straight fall (10), paid-yearly and adding against never pausing (11), multiplying e by the rate (12).
Rhythm: SHOW 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 alternate with DO 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; mixed puzzles 11 and 12; screen 13 is the brief's preview, a look ahead with no puzzle.
Terms: e and growth rate, two new terms, each used again in later lessons (the time constant and ln).
